title: Abetment of a thing
bareActText: A person abets the doing of a thing, who— (a) instigates any person to do that thing; or (b) engages with one or more other person or persons in any conspiracy for the doing of that thing, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing; or (c) intentionally aids, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing. Explanation 1.—A person who, by wilful misrepresentation, or by wilful concealment of a material fact which he is bound to disclose, voluntarily causes or procures, or attempts to cause or procure, a thing to be done, is said to instigate the doing of that thing. Illustration. A, a public officer, is authorised by a warrant from a Court to apprehend Z. B, knowing that fact and also that C is not Z, wilfully represents to A that C is Z, and thereby intentionally causes A to apprehend C. Here B abets by instigation the apprehension of C. Explanation 2.—Whoever, either prior to or at the time of the commission of an act, does anything in order to facilitate the commission of that act, and thereby facilitates the commission thereof, is said to aid the doing of that act.
plainMeaning: This section defines abetment. A person abets something in one of three ways: by instigating someone to do it; by joining a conspiracy to do it, where some act or illegal omission then happens in pursuance of that conspiracy; or by intentionally aiding it. Explanation 1 adds that instigation includes wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a material fact that one is bound to disclose. Explanation 2 says 'aiding' means doing something before or at the time of the act to facilitate it, and actually facilitating it.
ingredients: (a) Instigation of any person to do the thing, or
(b) Engaging in a conspiracy for doing it, plus an act or illegal omission in pursuance of that conspiracy, or
(c) Intentionally aiding the doing of it by an act or illegal omission
Instigation includes wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a material fact one is bound to disclose
Aid means facilitating, before or at the time of the act, and thereby actually facilitating it
punishment: Not applicable — this section defines abetment; punishment is set by ss.49-60.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.107 IPC; illustration now says 'a Court' instead of 'a Court of Justice'.

illustrations: R repeatedly urges and pressures S to set fire to a rival's shop, promising to pay him. R abets by instigation.
T lends U a ladder and keeps watch at the gate so that U can break into a house. T abets by intentional aid.

title: Abettor
bareActText: A person abets an offence, who abets either the commission of an offence, or the commission of an act which would be an offence, if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence with the same intention or knowledge as that of the abettor. Explanation 1.—The abetment of the illegal omission of an act may amount to an offence although the abettor may not himself be bound to do that act. Explanation 2.—To constitute the offence of abetment it is not necessary that the act abetted should be committed, or that the effect requisite to constitute the offence should be caused. Illustrations. (a) A instigates B to murder C. B refuses to do so. A is guilty of abetting B to commit murder. (b) A instigates B to murder D. B in pursuance of the instigation stabs D. D recovers from the wound. A is guilty of instigating B to commit murder. Explanation 3.—It is not necessary that the person abetted should be capable by law of committing an offence, or that he should have the same guilty intention or knowledge as that of the abettor, or any guilty intention or knowledge. Illustrations. (a) A, with a guilty intention, abets a child or a person of unsound mind to commit an act which would be an offence, if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence, and having the same intention as A. Here A, whether the act be committed or not, is guilty of abetting an offence. (b) A, with the intention of murdering Z, instigates B, a child under seven years of age, to do an act which causes Z’s death. B, in consequence of the abetment, does the act in the absence of A and thereby causes Z’s death. Here, though B was not capable by law of committing an offence, A is liable to be punished in the same manner as if B had been capable by law of committing an offence, and had committed murder, and he is therefore subject to the punishment of death. (c) A instigates B to set fire to a dwelling-house. B, in consequence of his unsoundness of mind, being incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is wrong or contrary to law, sets fire to the house in consequence of A’s instigation. B has committed no offence, but A is guilty of abetting the offence of setting fire to a dwelling-house, and is liable to the punishment provided for that offence. (d) A, intending to cause a theft to be committed, instigates B to take property belonging to Z out of Z’s possession. A induces B to believe that the property belongs to A. B takes the property out of Z’s possession, in good faith, believing it to be A’s property. B, acting under this misconception, does not take dishonestly, and therefore does not commit theft. But A is guilty of abetting theft, and is liable to the same punishment as if B had committed theft. Explanation 4.—The abetment of an offence being an offence, the abetment of such an abetment is also an offence. Illustration. A instigates B to instigate C to murder Z. B accordingly instigates C to murder Z, and C commits that offence in consequence of B’s instigation. B is liable to be punished for his offence with the punishment for murder; and, as A instigated B to commit the offence, A is also liable to the same punishment. Explanation 5.—It is not necessary to the commission of the offence of abetment by conspiracy that the abettor should concert the offence with the person who commits it. It is sufficient if he engages in the conspiracy in pursuance of which the offence is committed. Illustration. A concerts with B a plan for poisoning Z. It is agreed that A shall administer the poison. B then explains the plan to C mentioning that a third person is to administer the poison, but without mentioning A’s name. C agrees to procure the poison, and procures and delivers it to B for the purpose of its being used in the manner explained. A administers the poison; Z dies in consequence. Here, though A and C have not conspired together, yet C has been engaged in the conspiracy in pursuance of which Z has been murdered. C has therefore committed the offence defined in this section and is liable to the punishment for murder.
plainMeaning: An abettor is one who abets an offence, or an act that would be an offence if done by a person legally capable of committing it with the abettor's intention or knowledge. The Explanations make abetment very wide: abetting an illegal omission can be an offence even if the abettor was not himself bound to act; the abetted act need not actually be committed; the person abetted need not be capable of committing an offence or share any guilty mind; abetting an abetment is itself an offence; and in abetment by conspiracy the abettor need not deal directly with the person who commits the offence.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence, or of an act that would be an offence if done by a person capable by law with the abettor's intention or knowledge
Expl. 1 — abetting an illegal omission can be an offence though the abettor is not bound to act
Expl. 2 — the act abetted need not be committed, nor the effect caused
Expl. 3 — the person abetted need not be capable of an offence or have any guilty intention
Expl. 4 — abetment of an abetment is an offence
Expl. 5 — in conspiracy, the abettor need not concert with the person who commits the offence
punishment: Not applicable — this section defines an abettor; punishment is set by ss.49-60.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.108 IPC; wording and illustrations retained.

illustrations: V urges W to kill X. W refuses. V is still guilty of abetting murder, because the act abetted need not be committed.

title: Abetment in India of offences outside India
bareActText: A person abets an offence within the meaning of this Sanhita who, in India, abets the commission of any act without and beyond India which would constitute an offence if committed in India. Illustration. A, in India, instigates B, a foreigner in country X, to commit a murder in that country, A is guilty of abetting murder.
plainMeaning: A person who, while in India, abets an act done outside India is guilty of abetment under the Sanhita if that act would be an offence had it been done in India.
ingredients: The abetment takes place in India
The act abetted is done outside India
The act would be an offence if committed in India
punishment: Not applicable — this section extends abetment; punishment follows the relevant abetment section.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.108A IPC; wording retained.

illustrations: Z, sitting in Delhi, instigates a friend in Dubai to cheat a businessman there. Z is guilty of abetting cheating under the BNS.

title: Abetment outside India for offence in India
bareActText: A person abets an offence within the meaning of this Sanhita who, without and beyond India, abets the commission of any act in India which would constitute an offence if committed in India. Illustration. A, in country X, instigates B, to commit a murder in India, A is guilty of abetting murder.
plainMeaning: This is new in the BNS. A person who, while outside India, abets an act done in India is guilty of abetment under the Sanhita if that act would be an offence in India. It is the mirror image of s.47.
ingredients: The abetment takes place outside India
The act abetted is done in India
The act would be an offence if committed in India
punishment: Not applicable — this section extends abetment; punishment follows the relevant abetment section.

ipcReference.changeNote: New provision in the BNS: abetment from outside India of an offence in India.

illustrations: A person in another country sends money and instructions to a gang in Mumbai to commit a robbery there. He is guilty of abetting robbery under the BNS.

title: Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment
bareActText: Whoever abets any offence shall, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence. Explanation.—An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment, when it is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment. Illustrations. (a) A instigates B to give false evidence. B, in consequence of the instigation, commits that offence. A is guilty of abetting that offence, and is liable to the same punishment as B. (b) A and B conspire to poison Z. A, in pursuance of the conspiracy, procures the poison and delivers it to B in order that he may administer it to Z. B, in pursuance of the conspiracy, administers the poison to Z in A’s absence and thereby causes Z’s death. Here B is guilty of murder. A is guilty of abetting that offence by conspiracy, and is liable to the punishment for murder.
plainMeaning: If the abetted act is actually committed as a result of the abetment, and the Sanhita has no specific punishment for that abetment, the abettor gets the same punishment as for the offence itself. An act is 'in consequence of abetment' when it results from the instigation, happens in pursuance of the conspiracy, or is done with the aid that formed the abetment.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence
The act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment (instigation, conspiracy or aid)
No express provision punishes that particular abetment
punishment: Same punishment as provided for the offence abetted.

title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor
bareActText: Whoever abets the commission of an offence shall, if the person abetted does the act with a different intention or knowledge from that of the abettor, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence which would have been committed if the act had been done with the intention or knowledge of the abettor and with no other.
plainMeaning: If the person abetted does the act with a different intention or knowledge from the abettor's, the abettor is punished for the offence that would have been committed had the act been done with the abettor's own intention or knowledge. The abettor is judged by his own state of mind.
ingredients: Abetment of the commission of an offence
The person abetted acts with a different intention or knowledge
The abettor is punished as if the act had been done with his own intention or knowledge
punishment: Same punishment as for the offence abetted (judged by the abettor's intention or knowledge).

classification.bailable: According as the offence abetted is bailable or non-bailable
classification.compoundable: Only if the offence abetted is compoundable (BNSS s.359(3))
classification.triableBy: Court by which the offence abetted is triable

title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done
bareActText: When an act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the act done, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had directly abetted it: Provided that the act done was a probable consequence of the abetment, and was committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid or in pursuance of the conspiracy which constituted the abetment. Illustrations. (a) A instigates a child to put poison into the food of Z, and gives him poison for that purpose. The child, in consequence of the instigation, by mistake puts the poison into the food of Y, which is by the side of that of Z. Here, if the child was acting under the influence of A’s instigation, and the act done was under the circumstances a probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had instigated the child to put the poison into the food of Y. (b) A instigates B to burn Z’s house, B sets fire to the house and at the same time commits theft of property there. A, though guilty of abetting the burning of the house, is not guilty of abetting the theft; for the theft was a distinct act, and not a probable consequence of the burning. (c) A instigates B and C to break into an inhabited house at midnight for the purpose of robbery, and provides them with arms for that purpose. B and C break into the house, and being resisted by Z, one of the inmates, murder Z. Here, if that murder was the probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable to the punishment provided for murder.
plainMeaning: If the abettor abets one act but a different act is done, he is liable for the act actually done as if he had directly abetted it — but only if that act was a probable consequence of the abetment and was done under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid, or in pursuance of the conspiracy.
ingredients: One act is abetted but a different act is done
The act done was a probable consequence of the abetment
It was committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid, or in pursuance of the conspiracy
punishment: Same punishment as for the offence intended to be abetted (for the act actually done, within the proviso).

title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done
bareActText: If the act for which the abettor is liable under section 51 is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitute a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences. Illustration. A instigates B to resist by force a distress made by a public servant. B, in consequence, resists that distress. In offering the resistance, B voluntarily causes grievous hurt to the officer executing the distress. As B has committed both the offence of resisting the distress, and the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, B is liable to punishment for both these offences; and, if A knew that B was likely voluntarily to cause grievous hurt in resisting the distress, A will also be liable to punishment for each of the offences.
plainMeaning: Where, under s.51, the act done is in addition to the act abetted and is a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each offence separately.
ingredients: The abettor is liable under s.51 for an act done
That act is committed in addition to the act abetted
It constitutes a distinct offence
The abettor is punishable for each of the offences
punishment: Same punishment as for each offence abetted (cumulative).

title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor
bareActText: When an act is abetted with the intention on the part of the abettor of causing a particular effect, and an act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor, the abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect. Illustration. A instigates B to cause grievous hurt to Z. B, in consequence of the instigation, causes grievous hurt to Z. Z dies in consequence. Here, if A knew that the grievous hurt abetted was likely to cause death, A is liable to be punished with the punishment provided for murder.
plainMeaning: If the abetted act causes a different effect from the one the abettor intended, the abettor is liable for the effect actually caused, as if he had intended it — provided he knew the act abetted was likely to cause that effect.
ingredients: The abettor intended a particular effect
The act causes a different effect
The abettor knew the act abetted was likely to cause that effect
punishment: Same punishment as for the offence committed.

title: Abettor present when offence is committed
bareActText: Whenever any person, who is absent would be liable to be punished as an abettor, is present when the act or offence for which he would be punishable in consequence of the abetment is committed, he shall be deemed to have committed such act or offence.
plainMeaning: An abettor who would be liable even if absent, but who is actually present when the offence is committed, is treated as having committed the offence himself, not just abetted it.
ingredients: The person would be liable as an abettor even if absent
He is present when the act or offence is committed
He is deemed to have committed the act or offence
punishment: Same punishment as for the offence committed.

title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life
bareActText: Whoever abets the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made under this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if any act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, and which causes hurt to any person, is done, the abettor shall be liable to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and shall also be liable to fine. Illustration. A instigates B to murder Z. The offence is not committed. If B had murdered Z, he would have been subject to the punishment of death or imprisonment for life. Therefore, A is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and also to a fine; and if any hurt be done to Z in consequence of the abetment, he will be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and to fine.
plainMeaning: Abetting an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment is punishable even if that offence is not committed: up to seven years' imprisonment and fine. If an act done in consequence of the abetment causes hurt to anyone, the punishment rises to up to fourteen years and fine. This applies only where no specific provision punishes that abetment.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life
The offence is not committed in consequence of the abetment
No express provision punishes such abetment
Higher punishment if an act done in consequence causes hurt to any person
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 7 years, and fine. If hurt is caused: up to 14 years, and fine.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)

title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment
bareActText: Whoever abets an offence punishable with imprisonment shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made under this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term provided for that offence; or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; and if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, whose duty it is to prevent the commission of such offence, the abettor shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both. Illustrations. (a) A instigates B to give false evidence. Here, if B does not give false evidence, A has nevertheless committed the offence defined in this section, and is punishable accordingly. (b) A, a police officer, whose duty it is to prevent robbery, abets the commission of robbery. Here, though the robbery be not committed, A is liable to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, and also to fine. (c) B abets the commission of a robbery by A, a police officer, whose duty it is to prevent that offence. Here, though the robbery be not committed, B is liable to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence of robbery, and also to fine.
plainMeaning: Abetting an offence punishable with imprisonment is itself punishable even if the offence is not committed: up to one-fourth of the longest term for that offence, or its fine, or both. If the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant whose duty it is to prevent that offence, the limit rises to one-half of the longest term.
ingredients: Abetment of an offence punishable with imprisonment
The offence is not committed in consequence of the abetment
No express provision punishes such abetment
Higher limit (one-half) if the abettor or person abetted is a public servant whose duty is to prevent the offence
punishment: Up to one-fourth of the longest term for the offence, or fine, or both. If a public servant whose duty is to prevent the offence is involved: up to one-half of the longest term, or fine, or both.

title: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons
bareActText: Whoever abets the commission of an offence by the public generally or by any number or class of persons exceeding ten, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years and with fine. Illustration. A affixes in a public place a placard instigating a sect consisting of more than ten members to meet at a certain time and place, for the purpose of attacking the members of an adverse sect, while engaged in a procession. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
plainMeaning: Abetting an offence by the public in general, or by any number or class of more than ten persons, is a separate offence punishable with up to seven years and fine. It targets mass instigation.
ingredients: Abetment of the commission of an offence
By the public generally, or by any number or class of persons exceeding ten
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 7 years, and fine.

classification.cognizable: According as the offence abetted is cognizable or non-cognizable
classification.bailable: According as the offence abetted is bailable or non-bailable
classification.compoundable: Not listed in BNSS s.359 (s.359(3) allows compounding abetment of an offence that is itself compoundable)
classification.triableBy: Court by which the offence abetted is triable

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.117 IPC; wording retained. The punishment is raised from up to 3 years, or fine, or both, to up to 7 years and a compulsory fine.

illustrations: TT posts a message in a large online group urging its members to gather and attack members of another community during a festival. TT is guilty under s.57.

title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life
bareActText: Whoever intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, voluntarily conceals by any act or omission, or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit such offence or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design shall,–– (a) if that offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years; or (b) if the offence be not committed, with imprisonment of either description, for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine. Illustration. A, knowing that dacoity is about to be committed at B, falsely informs the Magistrate that a dacoity is about to be committed at C, a place in an opposite direction, and thereby misleads the Magistrate with intent to facilitate the commission of the offence. The dacoity is committed at B in pursuance of the design. A is punishable under this section.
plainMeaning: Hiding the existence of a plan to commit an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment — or making a false statement about it — intending to help it happen, or knowing it is likely to help, is punishable. It covers concealment by any act or omission, and now expressly by encryption or any other information-hiding tool. Punishment is up to seven years if the offence is committed, and up to three years and fine if it is not.
ingredients: Intending to facilitate, or knowing it likely to facilitate, an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment
Voluntarily conceals the existence of the design (by act, omission, encryption or other information-hiding tool), or makes a representation he knows is false about it
(a) offence committed: up to 7 years
(b) offence not committed: up to 3 years and fine
punishment: (a) If the offence is committed: imprisonment of either description up to 7 years. (b) If not committed: up to 3 years, and fine.

classification.cognizable: According as the offence abetted is cognizable or non-cognizable
classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)
classification.triableBy: Court by which the offence abetted is triable

illustrations: UU knows a gang plans a dacoity on the highway tonight and deliberately tells the police it will happen in a different town, so that the gang can succeed. UU is guilty under s.58.
VV stores a group's detailed murder plan on an encrypted drive and deletes the key when police ask for it, to protect the plan. This is concealment by encryption.

title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent
bareActText: Whoever, being a public servant, intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence which it is his duty as such public servant to prevent, voluntarily conceals, by any act or omission or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit such offence, or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design shall,–– (a) if the offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term of such imprisonment, or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; or (b) if the offence be punishable with death or imprisonment for life, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years; or (c) if the offence be not committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term of such imprisonment or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both. Illustration. A, an officer of police, being legally bound to give information of all designs to commit robbery which may come to his knowledge, and knowing that B designs to commit robbery, omits to give such information, with intent to so facilitate the commission of that offence. Here A has by an illegal omission concealed the existence of B’s design, and is liable to punishment according to the provision of this section.
plainMeaning: A public servant who hides the existence of a plan to commit an offence that it is his duty to prevent — or makes a false statement about it — intending to help it, or knowing it is likely to help, is punishable more heavily than an ordinary person. Concealment includes encryption or any other information-hiding tool.
ingredients: The accused is a public servant whose duty is to prevent the offence
Intending to facilitate, or knowing it likely to facilitate, the offence
Voluntarily conceals the design (by act, omission, encryption or other tool), or makes a false representation about it
(a) offence committed: up to one-half of the longest term, or fine, or both
(b) offence punishable with death or life imprisonment: up to 10 years
(c) offence not committed: up to one-fourth of the longest term, or fine, or both
punishment: (a) If the offence is committed: up to one-half of the longest term, or fine, or both. (b) If the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment: up to 10 years. (c) If not committed: up to one-fourth of the longest term, or fine, or both.

title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment
bareActText: Whoever, intending to facilitate or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby facilitate the commission of an offence punishable with imprisonment, voluntarily conceals, by any act or illegal omission, the existence of a design to commit such offence, or makes any representation which he knows to be false respecting such design shall,–– (a) if the offence be committed, be punished with imprisonment of the description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-fourth; and (b) if the offence be not committed, to one-eighth, of the longest term of such imprisonment, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.
plainMeaning: Hiding the existence of a plan to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment — or making a false statement about it — intending to help it, or knowing it is likely to help, is punishable: up to one-fourth of the longest term if the offence is committed, and up to one-eighth if it is not, or the offence's fine, or both.
ingredients: Intending to facilitate, or knowing it likely to facilitate, an offence punishable with imprisonment
Voluntarily conceals the design by act or illegal omission, or makes a false representation about it
(a) offence committed: up to one-fourth of the longest term
(b) offence not committed: up to one-eighth of the longest term; or fine, or both
punishment: (a) If the offence is committed: up to one-fourth of the longest term. (b) If not committed: up to one-eighth of the longest term; or fine, or both.

title: Criminal conspiracy
bareActText: (1) When two or more persons agree with the common object to do, or cause to be done–– (a) an illegal act; or (b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof. Explanation.—It is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of such agreement, or is merely incidental to that object. (2) Whoever is a party to a criminal conspiracy,–– (a) to commit an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term of two years or upwards, shall, where no express provision is made in this Sanhita for the punishment of such a conspiracy, be punished in the same manner as if he had abetted such offence; (b) other than a criminal conspiracy to commit an offence punishable as aforesaid shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding six months, or with fine or with both.
plainMeaning: A criminal conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons, with the common object of doing an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means. An agreement to commit an offence is a conspiracy by itself; any other agreement becomes one only when some act is done in pursuance of it. Punishment: for a conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment of two years or more, the same as abetment of that offence (unless a specific provision applies); for any other conspiracy, up to six months, or fine, or both.
ingredients: An agreement between two or more persons
With the common object of doing an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means
If the agreement is not to commit an offence, some act besides the agreement must be done in pursuance of it
It does not matter whether the illegal act is the ultimate object or merely incidental
(2)(a) conspiracy to commit a serious offence (death, life, or RI of 2 years or more): punished as abetment of that offence
(2)(b) any other conspiracy: up to 6 months, or fine, or both
punishment: (2)(a) For a conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or RI of 2 years or more: as if the offender had abetted that offence. (2)(b) Any other: imprisonment of either description up to 6 months, or fine, or both.

classification.cognizable: (2)(a) According as the offence which is the object of the conspiracy is cognizable or non-cognizable; (2)(b) Non-cognizable
classification.bailable: (2)(a) According as the object offence is bailable or non-bailable; (2)(b) Bailable
classification.triableBy: (2)(a) Court by which abetment of the object offence is triable; (2)(b) Magistrate of the first class

ipcReference.changeNote: Combines the definition (s.120A) and punishment (s.120B) of criminal conspiracy into one section; BNS adds the words 'with the common object'.

illustrations: YY and ZZ agree to kidnap a businessman's child for ransom and start watching the family's house. Their agreement to commit an offence is already a criminal conspiracy, and they are punished as abettors of kidnapping.

Two traders agree to raise prices by spreading a false rumour of shortage. Since this is not an agreement to commit an offence under the BNS, it becomes a criminal conspiracy only once they actually spread the rumour.

title: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment
bareActText: Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Sanhita with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission of the offence, shall, where no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such attempt, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the imprisonment for life or, as the case may be, one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both. Illustrations. (a) A makes an attempt to steal some jewels by breaking open a box, and finds after so opening the box, that there is no jewel in it. He has done an act towards the commission of theft, and therefore is guilty under this section. (b) A makes an attempt to pick the pocket of Z by thrusting his hand into Z’s pocket. A fails in the attempt in consequence of Z’s having nothing in his pocket. A is guilty under this section.
plainMeaning: Where the Sanhita has no specific provision for the attempt, attempting an offence punishable with life imprisonment or imprisonment — and doing any act towards committing it — is punishable with up to one-half of life imprisonment, or one-half of the longest term, or the offence's fine, or both. An attempt can be punished even if the offence was impossible in the circumstances, such as picking an empty pocket.
ingredients: Attempt to commit (or cause to be committed) an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment
Doing any act towards the commission of the offence (beyond mere preparation)
No express provision punishes that attempt
Up to one-half of life imprisonment, or one-half of the longest term; or fine; or both
punishment: Up to one-half of imprisonment for life, or one-half of the longest term provided for the offence; or fine; or both.

classification.cognizable: According as the offence attempted is cognizable or non-cognizable
classification.bailable: According as the offence attempted is bailable or non-bailable
classification.compoundable: Only if the offence attempted is compoundable (BNSS s.359(3))
classification.triableBy: Court by which the offence attempted is triable

illustrations: AB breaks into a locked car to steal a laptop, but finds the car empty. He has done an act towards theft and is guilty of attempted theft.
AC only buys a crowbar and studies a shop's layout, intending to break in later. That is preparation, not yet an attempt.
